full_judgment:
Anwarul Hoque Chowdhury, J.---This Rule arise out an application under section 561 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure for quashing the proceeding in sessions case No 5 of 1983 pending before Additional District Magistrate, Jessore arising out of Jessore Sadar, D.A.B. G.R.No. 16 of 1982 and Kotwali P.S. Case No. 25 dated 12-6.82 under sections 468/419/420/471 and read with section 109 of the Penal Code. 

 2. Facts leading to this Rule in short are that Opposite parties Mst. Halima Khatun, wife of late Sadaruddin Ahmed and Hosne Ara, wife of Abdul Wahed Khan of village Kandra of PS Jhenidah, District Jessore submitted a petition to the Bureau of Anti-Corruption, Jessore to the effect that petitioner Mst. Saleha Khatun wife of Hazi Manirussamah of village Kandra under PS Jhenidah, District Jessore in connivance with others had created a false document namely a Bainanama showing one Sadaraddin Ahmed husband of the complainant Halima Khatun as executor of the said Bainapatra and for specific performance of that Contract a suit was filed in the Court of Subordinate Judge Jessore being O/C suit No. 152/80 dated 18-12-80. The said Bainapatra is false one as it was never created by the husband of the complainant. This complaint was endorsed to the Assistant Inspector of Anti-corruption Bureau, Jessore for inquiry and the laid Asstt. Inspector DAB Jessore inquired into the matter, seized the questioned Bainapatra from file of OC suit No. 152/80 under order of the learned District and Sessions Judge sent the questioned Bainanama to CID for expert opinion. The hand-writing expert of CID Dhaka opined that the questioned Bainapatra is out and out a forged document. On receipt of the said report from Dhaka the said Assistant Inspector DAB. Jessore suo motu started the police case being GR Case No. 16/82 and examined the witnesses, recorded their statements under section 161 CrPC seized other connected papers end also ex-accused and found prima-facie case against accused persons namely, petitioner Mst. Saleha Khatun, Asadul Alam, Md. Abdul Hossain, Md Tanjilur Rahman. Montu Mohuri Mofazzel Hossain, Koton, Md Shamsuddin Md. Osman Ghani under sections 468/471/419/ 420/109 of the Bangladesh Penal Code to the effect that accused Asadul Alam, Mst. Saleha and Abdul Hossain tried to obtain wrongful gain by deceitful means and fraudulently and accused No. 5 Tanjilur Rahman for engineering the whole misdeeds and accused No. 5-7 abetted by witnessing the creation of the false Bainapatra, knowing fully in advance that it was a forged document. The said charge-sheet was submitted on 2-11-82 by the said Assistant Inspector DAB Jessore. Accordingly, the case was started in the Court of Sub-divisional Magistrate Jessore, the sole petitioner before this Court Mst. Saleha Khatun surrendered before the Court with a petition for bail which was granted. 

 3. The Sub-Divisional Magistrate thereafter sent the case record to the learned Sessions Judge on 2-1-83 for trial. The case was numbered as Sessions Case No. 5 of 1983. Before that Court she entered appearance on 11-1-83 when the learned Sessions Judge was pleased to allow the petitioner to continue on bail already granted. It is the further case of the petitioner, as stated in the para 6 of the petition, that the petitioner is the full sister of Sadaruddin Biswas, the executor of the alleged Bainapatra in favour of the sister for sale of his property and the said brother is the husband of the informant Halima Khatun. It is the case that the petitioner on 9-12-72 filed a partition suit against her brother, the executor of the alleged bainanama and others in the court of Munsif 2nd Court Jhenidah but the defendant namely her brother, and all others co-shareres in spite of notice did not appear and on 9-12-75 the partition suit was decreed ex-pane. It was objected to by the defendants, on appeal it was dismissed and the petitioners accordingly has been possessing peacefully her share she acquired through that partition decree. When that was the case opposite party No. 2 being Mst. Halima Khatun, wife of petitioner's brother, filed a suit in the year 1980 in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Jessore on the allegation that petitioner Mst. Saleha Khatun on 22-11-52 executed a power of attorney in favour of one Moniruzzaman Khan and divested herself of the right, title and interest in the ejmali property. The said ex parte decree in favour of Saleha Khatun in Title Suit No. 342 of 1972 was void and illegal, she having no subsisting interest and that Halima Khatun has become 16 annas owner of the entire property as Saleha Khatun divested her interest in favour of one Moniruzzaman and it is Halima who is in possession of the entire properties left by father of both Saleha Khatun and her husband and in that view of the matter she prayed for partition of her 16 annas share. 

 4. This petitioner before us and another sister Aklima Khatun entered appearance in that case and stated that there existed no such power of attorney in favour of Moniruzzaman Khan when Halima Khatun started putting pressure on the petitioner for compromise on terms of Halima Khatun but the petitioner having refused to submit to the pressure the informant Halim Khatun engineered a bogus suit being O.C. Suit No. 112 of 1982 in the Court of the Subordinate Judge Jessore in which the said petitioner Saleha was shown as plaintiff and Halima Khatun (Opposite party No. 2) as defendant No. 1. The suit was filed with a court fee of Taka 100 for specific performance of contract of an alleged unregistered Bainanama when the petitioner never filed such suit nor did she sign any plaint, verification or Vokalatoama and she knows nothings of the OC Suit No, 152 of 1980. When that was the case the Assistant Inspector, DAB Jessore on 17-2-81 filed a petition for seizure of the unregistered bainanama which was allowed. The petitioner coming to know of the FIR surrendered before the Sub-divisional Magistrate, Jessore where she stated that she never filed any such suit and she filed a petition before the Sub-divisional Magistrate Jessore stating that the Investigation Officer is vitally interested in the case as he is related to Halima Khatun having intimate relations as friends and she made other allegation against the investigating officer also. 

 5. The petitioner also requested the authority for sending the signature of the alleged executor to the handwriting expert which was ignored, thereafter, the petitioner submitted written representation to the Deputy Commissioner Jessore and to Director Anti-corruption Dhaka to send the signature for expert opinion and to replace the investigation officer but to no result. Thereafter, the petitioner appeared before the Sessions Judge, Jessore on 11-1-83 and submitted that the trial of the accused in the circumstances of the case is without jurisdiction and, as much, as the Subordinate Judge in whose Court OC Suit No. 152 of 1980 was pending did not file the complaint and the trial hits section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Learned Sessions Judge ordered to put the application on the next date 24-1-83 when she filed another application for, sending the alleged signature of the executor for expert opinion the prayer was rejected. On 24-1-83 the petitioner filed another application for calling for the alleged unregistered bainanama. The said was also rejected. On 30-1-83 the case was transferred to the Additional District Magistrate where it is now pending. It is alleged by the petitioner that the FIR was lodged suo motu and the investigation officer is an interested police officer and that no prima-facie case is revealed from the FIR and the charge-sheet. The case has been created by the opposite parties Nos. 2 and 3 in collusion with the complainant Investigation Officer only to harass and put pressure upon the petitioner to nullify the exparte decree passed in Title Suite No. 354 of 1972 and only to pressurise her in Title Suit No.8 of 1980 and to compromise on their terms. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid Criminal Proceeding in sessions Case No. 5 of 1983 the petitioner has moved this Court for quashing of the same and obtained this Rule. 

 6. Mr Muhammad Abdul Hoque, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner having taken us through the petition and the various exhibits being Annexure A, FIR Annexure A Charge-sheet, (Annexure B) partition suit decree (Annexure 'C') the plaint of the suit being TS No. 8 of 1980 filed by Halima Khatun and the plaint of OC suit No. 152/80 including order sheets covered by Annexure which are receipts of registered letters issued by post office and having done so, submitted in great details, to the effect that this is a fit case for quashment because it amounts to harassment of the petitioner, in view of the malafide actions of interested police officer. It amounts thus, to an abuse of the process of the court and needs to be quashed in limini. In elaborating this point Mr Mohammad Abdul Hoque, the learned Advocate for petitioner submits there is no prima facie case revealed from the FIR and the charge-sheet. He has next submitted that the charge-sheet was created in collusion with an interested officer without any materials. He had further submitted that the writer of the alleged Bainanama and identifier of the executant of the said unregistered document being not cited as accused in the case the charge-sheet on the face of it is malafide, made with an ulterior motive to harass the petitioner and, as such, it is liable to be quashed. He has lastly submitted that the complaint having been lodged illegally without moving the learned Subordinate Judge, to lodge such a complaint offends section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and hence it cannot proceed and thus is liable to be quashed. 

 7. Mr AH Mahfoozur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party Nos. 2 and 3 Mst. Halima Khatun and Husneara submitted that this rule has no substance and the petitioner cannot ask to quash a proceeding as a matter of right but only when the allegations made against an accused was absurd or perverse disclosing no offence in the eye of law. In the present case the FIR as submitted, disclosed an offence which if proved is punishable under the law. Hence, it cannot be said that it is a fit case for quashing. 

 8. This is an application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure for quashing the proceeding started against the petitioner in Sessions Case No. 5 of 1983 now pending before the Additional District Magistrate Jessore under 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The High Court exercises its inherent power to avoid any abuse of the process of the Court or to secure the ends of justice. Hence out of necessity it requires a finding to the effect that if the proceeding is permitted to continue it would defeat the ends of justice and would operate to perpetuate injustice and also that it would amount to an abuse of the process of the court. The High Court would be extremely reluctant to interfere in a case where, a competent court came to the view that a prima facie case is disclosed and had framed a charge in view of that prima facie case, unless it could be shown that the charge-sheet on its face, even if believed did not disclose any offence. To quash a proceeding on any other ground would amount to stifling the proceeding before the prosecution would have any opportunity to prove its case. The court might be acting on treacherous ground in quashing a criminal proceeding at the interlocutory stage or early stage on the ground that continuation of the proceeding would be an abuse of the process of the Court and the Court would be extremely reluctant to interfere unless it can be said that, the allegation that has been made in the FIR or charges framed on the ground even if believed would not disclose an offence under any of the provisions of the Penal Code, then only a question of abuse of process would arise so also the ends of Justice (ref : 31 DLR Page 39). 

 9. The point before us is whether the fact stated in the FIR and also the charge-sheet disclosed a prima facie case against the petitioner or not. There is an allegation against the Investigation Officer to the effect that he has acted malafide in the matter of investigation and the charge-sheet but that would not mean that the charges as framed against the complainant would not disclose an offence because of the malafide action of the investigation officer unless the malafide action is proved first. The charge-sheet stated that there is an allegation to the effect that the accused in connivance with others had created a false bainanama in her favour showing one Mr Sadaruddin Biswas, husband of the petitioner Mst. Halima Khatun as executor of the bainanama. It further reveals that the inquiry officer of the Anti-Corruption Department seized the questioned bainanama from the fill of the suit being suit No. 152/80 under order of the learned District & Sessions Judge, Jessore and sent the questioned Bainanama to CID for expert opinion and handwriting expert at Dhaka and they opined that the questioned Bainanama is out and out a forged deed of contract and a suo motu case was started and during investigation Assistant Inspector of DAB examined case records and found a prima-facie case. The charge-sheet thereafter is submitted against the accused under the sections of the Penal Code, mentioned herein before and it categorically mentions that accused Nos. 1, 2 and 3 are liable to be tried for having wrongful gain by deceitful means & fraudulently, accused No. 4 for engineering the whole misdeed and 5-7 for abetment in creating the false bainanama. There is no allegation, it appears from the charge-sheet, that the said bainanama is being created for the purpose of a proceeding when pending before a Court by any of the parties as such for the purpose of the suit and there is no allegation that this false bainanama had been used in relation to a proceeding in court of law. 

 10. Section 468 speaks of a substantive offence for forgery and section 468 speaks of an offence of forgery for the purpose of cheating. It provided that whoever commits forgery intending that the document forged shall be used for the purpose of cheating shall be punished with imprisonment for 7 years and also be liable to fine. If the guilty purpose in creating the document was to cheat, the offence would be complete. That was the first charge-sheet against accused petitioner to the effect that she along with other committed forgery by making false document for the purpose of cheating ie obtaining property dishonestly and fraudulently. And in the instant case if the signature would be proved to be a forged signature the offence would be complete, punishable under the law. But the finding of fact has not yet been arrived at. Second charge was under section 471 which speaks of using as genuine a forged document and 471 clearly provided that whoever fraudulently or dishonestly, which means with a guilty mind to cheat, uses as genuine a document be knows to be forged be punishable in the same manner as if he has forged such a document. The next charge is under section 419 which provided for punishment for the offence of cheating by personation related to the substantive offence as under section 419 which provides that a persons is said to cheat by personation if he cheats by pretending to be some other person, or by knowingly substitutes one person for another or representing that he or any other person is the person other than he or such other persons really is. All these relates to the offence of signing the document pretending to be another person. That is a questions of fact. Next charge is under section 420, which speaks of cheating and also dishonestly inducing delivery of property. Hence, on a reading of the F.I.R. and the charge-sheet we are of the opinion that there is an offence found prima facie by police as in the FIR. The charge-sheet disclosed a prima facie offence. That being the position it could not be said that the FIR or the Charge-sheet did not disclose any offence or any prima facie offence against the accused for the proceeding to be quashed, being an abuse of the process of the court and for securing the ends of justice. 

 11. This matter as to the power of the High Court under section 561A of the Code has been elaborately discussed by their lordships of this Court in the case of MG Towab vs The State, reported in 35 DLR at page 371. The said Criminal Revision No. 410 of 1981 filed by MG Towab against the State was heard by a Division Bench of this Court but their lordships having differed the matter was referred to a third Judge under section 429 CrPC and his lordship presiding over the second single Bench concurring with the observation of his lordship Mr Justice ATM Afzal, held in the relevant portion of the judgment thus: " 

 12. "Many accused persons in this country do not understand the limited scope of the inherent power of this Court under section 561A, CrPC and very often compel their lawyers to come up with these petitions with the hope that this Court will go beyond the FIR and the charge-sheet and accept the defence version of the case ex-parts and quash the Criminal proceedings against them. I cannot but agree with my learned brother ATM Afzal, J. when he says, I have taken pains to point out the difficulty and the legal position for which this court cannot and should not embark upon examining the myriad of facts which have been alleged by the petitioner nor can we ask the prosecution to lead evidence before us". 

 13. In that view of the matter his lordship found no ground under section 561A for quashing the Criminal proceeding pending against the petitioner on a finding that the charge as framed disclosed a prima facie case as in the FIR for criminal misconduct against the accused petitioner as defined under section 1(d) Act II of 1947 and for that the charge-sheet submitted by the prosecution could not be said that it is a case of no evidence. 

 15. We are in complete agreement with the views of his Lordship Mr ATM Afzal and Mr Mohammad Habibur Rahman, J as in Towab's case, reported in 34 DLR at page 371-402. That being the position in the instant case there is no lack of prima-facie case as disclosed in the FIR and the Charge sheet that the accused petitioner has allegedly committed some offence and if proved would call for punishment under the law and therefore no interference is called for with the proceeding by this Court at this stage. 

 16. Next, we come to the question of the embargo as to initiating a complaint Case as laid down under section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It is urged by the learned Counsel before us that this proceeding was also not competent because in whose court the alleged bainanama is said to have been submitted had not made any complaint as required under section 195(c) of the Code and in the absence of such a complaint by the Court the proceeding started for using a false document in a proceeding before a Court is barred under section 195(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Hence, it is argued that the proceeding is liable to be quashed. 

 20. In the view we have taken in this regard reference may be made to a decision of a Special Bench of the Allahabad High Court, reported in AIR 1931, at page 443. In that case under report their Lordships decided a question when the alleged document was forged long before one of the accused became a party to a proceeding where the document was used. Mukerji, J. in delivering the judgment in the relevant portion observed thus; 

 "Which appears to have been committed in or in relation to a proceeding in the Court" with reference to an offence referred to in section 195, if then, it be the case then, section 195 lays down the bar and section 476 lays down the method for removing the bar. I take it, we must lead the two sections together. 

 It has been urged that section 476 may not be exhaustive and it may be open to a Court to file a complaint although it may not be possible for it to file a complaint under section 476, Criminal PC. This argument does not appeal to me and for various reasons. A Court is a creature of law and can act only in the manner laid down in law. Abstract notions of justice cannot persuade a Court to act contrary to rules laid down by law. Further, the responsibility of initiating prosecution is immense. A person who takes upon himself the responsibility of initiating a prosecution may be himself prosecuted if is found that the prosecution was lightly and without sufficient cause launched, or if there was a malice in his mind. He may be civilly liable in damages. In the case of complaint by the Court all this is not possible and even when the prosecution fails the person prosecuted has no remedy. If therefore a person is to have no remedy it is necessary that a Court should act within the rule of law laid down for its guidance and not outside it. 

 As to inherent Jurisdiction it cannot be said that a Court, specially a Civil Court, has an inherent jurisdiction to file a complaint. That is not the ordinary function of a civil or any Court. The power to file a complaint is given by the Criminal Procedure Code and this does not indicate existence of any inherent jurisdiction, except that of a High Court section 561A. But if we lay down that there is a power to make a complaint outside section 476, Criminal PC we must lay it down for subordinate Courts also section 151. Civil PC cannot be read as authorizing the filing of criminal complaint, a matter which is not at all dealt with in that Code. It seems to me therefore to be tolerably clear that a complaint, outside the provisions of section 476, cannot be filed by civil, revenue or criminal Court under its inherent jurisdiction. This being my opinion, I would read section 476 and clause (c) section 195, as having the same scope. In other words I would read clause (c), section 195, so as to make it comprehensive or offences which would be outside the purview of section 476, unless the language is such as would compel me to put a construction which can-not be reconciled in the manner indicated ; Going back to the language of clause (c) section 195(1). I find that the offence should be one which has been committed by a party to proceeding. Now an office which has already been committed by a person who does not become a party till, say 30 years after the commission of the offence, cannot be said to have been committed "by a party" within the meaning of clause (c). The word "party" must mean a party and nothing else. If we lay a little emphasis on the word "party" or if we add the words "as such" after the word "party", the meaning of clause (c) would be quite in keeping with the provision of section 476 Criminal P C. Let us consider some of the consequences that would follow if we give a wider interpretation to clause (c) section 195, when a civil or revenue or a criminal court, not being a Court of highest jurisdiction, proceeds under section 476 an appeal is provided for and the proceeding is subject to re-examination by the appellate Court. If there by any case to which section I95(1)(c) is applicable and to which section 476 does net apply, the result would be that there will be some offences for which a Court would be entitled to file a complaint, (assuming that a Court can file a complaint), but there will be no check by way or an appeal in those cases. It can hardly have been contemplated by the legislature that, while it deliberately provided for appeals in some cases, it failed to provide for appeals in certain other cases. Before the amendment of 1923 every sanction to prosecute, granted by a Court under section 195 (1) (c) was appealable. 

 For these reasons I would hold that clause (c) section 195, applies only to cases where an offence is committed by a party, as such, to a proceeding in any Court in respect of a document which has been produced or given in evidence in such proceeding. 

 In this view of the law, the documents which we have to consider could not come within the purview of section 195(1)(c). These documents were forged (supposing they were forged) some time in 1898 and by a person who did not become a party to the present proceedings till the year 1922 when the suit was filed. My answer therefore to the question is in the negative. We are in respectful agreement with the observation of their Lordships, which are in complete accord with the view we have taken hereinbefore. We find that in the instant case the alleged forged document was a alleged to have been forged on 8-1-80 by the petitioner Mst. Saleha Khatun in collusion with others and she became a party to a proceeding for specific performance of that bainanama in O/C Suit No. 157/80, almost after 12 months thereafter, which filling of the suit she now clearly denies and which proceeding has now come to an end being dismissed for default. The alleged forgery was committed allegedly by the petitioner according to the police and the complainant along with 5 others when they were thus, not a party to any proceeding. The alleged offence or forgery would be complete when the document is created with the malafide intention as under the law without, itself being used in a Court. Further, it is seen from the FIR that no allegation has been made there to the effect that they committed an offence for having used these in a court or law. Further, the charge-sheet clearly stated that the accused persons would be tried under sections 468/471/419/420/109 Penal Code, accused No. 5 for dishonestly and fraudulently engineering the same, accused Nos. 5-7 for abetment of the same and the allegation was not that they committed the offence by forging a document for the purpose of a proceeding when they have been a party to that proceeding, in which case the provisions of section 195 would have been immediately attracted. That being the position, in the facts and circumstances of the case, the provision of section 195 (c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not applicable. Hence, the proceeding started and pending before the learned Sessions Judge could not be said to be a proceeding pending against the petitioner which need to be quashed being a proceeding offending the provisions of section 195(c) CrPC.
